fetched_contents.text: Types of abortion An abortion (also known as a termination) is the medical process of ending a pregnancy. An abortion is different from a miscarriage, which is the loss of your baby before 24 weeks, without medical intervention. Read more about how to access an abortion in Scotland There are 2 types of abortion: * medical, which uses medication * surgical, which involves a small operation Before undergoing any type of abortion, you’ll be asked to give consent to proceed. Medical abortion This involves you taking 2 sets of tablets at different times. You may be able to take 1 or both sets of tablets at home, depending on your circumstances. When you’ve your initial assessment appointment, you’ll be advised what is appropriate for you. Starting the abortion To start the abortion, you’ll swallow a tablet called mifepristone. This blocks the hormones that allow pregnancy to continue. After taking mifepristone, you can carry on with your normal daily activities. Some people do feel side effects after taking mifepristone. These can include: * a headache * nausea * vomiting * diarrhoea * bleeding If you vomit less than 2 hours after taking your tablet, contact your local health board abortion service immediately. You’ll need to take more. Completing the abortion 36 to 48 hours after taking mifepristone, you’ll take the first dose of misoprostol. There are different ways of taking misoprostol tablets, including: * placing the tablet under your tongue for 30 minutes * placing the tablet inside the vagina Your local health board abortion service will give you advice on exactly when and how to take misoprostol. Follow their instructions carefully. You may need to take further doses of misoprostol if you’ve not experienced any bleeding, or only have very light bleeding after 4 hours. It’s normal to experience uncomfortable symptoms after taking misoprostol. Different people have different experiences, but people often have: * cramps that are more intense than your usual period * heavy bleeding * passing blood clots The pregnancy sac will pass with the clots. Your local health board abortion service will give you painkillers to take as needed. You can also take ibuprofen or paracetamol up to the recommended safe dose. A hot water bottle or heat pack can also provide some relief. These symptoms normally settle and improve after 4-6 hours, although it can take longer for some people. Where can I have a medical abortion? You may be able to take 1 or both types of medications at home. This is called Early Medical Abortion at Home (EMAH). If this option is right for you, you may be asked to collect your medication pack from your local health board abortion service. You can also ask the service can deliver it to you if you prefer. You’ll be given information on how and when to take your tablets. Make sure you understand the instructions and follow them. EMAH is not right for everybody. In some circumstances, you may be asked to take 1 or both of your tablets in a clinic or hospital. This commonly happens because you: * have medical conditions that mean it’d be better for you to be in hospital * do not want to have your abortion at home After taking your second (misoprostol) tablets in the hospital, you’ll stay there until the pregnancy has passed. This occasionally requires an overnight stay. Surgical abortion You may be offered the option of a surgical abortion. This can be done under: * general anaesthetic (where you are asleep) * sedation (where you are awake, but drowsy) * local anaesthetic (where the cervix involved is numbed by injection, but you’re fully awake) Surgical abortions involve removing the pregnancy through the cervix using gentle suction. The procedure usually takes about 10 minutes. Mifepristone is not usually required for a surgical abortion. You may be asked to take misoprostol to prepare the cervix for the procedure. After the procedure, you’ll stay in hospital for a few hours to make sure you’ve recovered enough to go home. Normally, you’ll be able to go home the same day. Abortion after 20 weeks In some circumstances, people who need an abortion after 20 weeks of pregnancy will be referred to specialist services in England. Your local health board abortion service should provide help with travel and accommodation costs. If you’re more than 22 weeks pregnant, the abortion usually requires a two-stage procedure. In stage 1, you’ll be given an injection to stop the heartbeat of the fetus and medication to soften the cervix (opening of the womb). Stage 2 is carried out the following day. You’ll have surgery to remove the pregnancy (the fetus and surrounding tissue). Following the procedure you’ll bleed, usually for up to 14 days. You may notice some other symptoms, like a small amount of fluid leaking from your breasts. After an abortion If you’ve had an abortion, whether surgical or medical, you’ll be given a pregnancy test. You should take this 14 or 21 days after the procedure to check that it’s been successful. There are more likely to be issues if an abortion is carried out later in a pregnancy. fetched_contents.text: Mifepristone - StatPearls Continuing Education Activity Mifepristone, also called RU-486, is a synthetic steroid with dual FDA-approved applications. Firstly, it is utilized in combination with misoprostol for pregnancy termination up to 10 weeks of gestation, offering a medical alternative to surgical procedures for induced abortions. Secondly, mifepristone is employed in managing and treating hyperglycemia associated with Cushing syndrome. As a low-dose competitive binder, mifepristone obstructs progesterone action by binding to its intracellular receptor. Higher doses impede cortisol activity at the glucocorticoid receptor, concurrently elevating circulating cortisol levels to regulate hyperglycemia in individuals with Cushing syndrome. Apart from its predominant use in medically induced abortions, mifepristone proves valuable in addressing Cushing syndrome and uterine leiomyomas. This activity focuses on elucidating the mechanism of action, adverse event profile, and other crucial aspects, such as dosing, pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, monitoring, and relevant interactions of mifepristone. Healthcare professionals treating patients with mifepristone gain insights into its multifaceted roles, facilitating informed decision-making within the healthcare team. Noteworthy adverse reactions associated with mifepristone include bacterial infections and prolonged, heavy menstrual bleeding, underscoring the importance of comprehensive understanding and vigilance in its clinical use. Objectives: * Identify appropriate indications for mifepristone use in elective abortion procedures and other medical conditions. * Screen patients to assess their eligibility for mifepristone therapy, considering medical history, contraindications, and potential drug interactions. * Assess patient response to mifepristone treatment and monitor for adverse reactions or complications. * Develop effective communication with patients, providing clear instructions and addressing their concerns regarding mifepristone treatment. Access free multiple choice questions on this topic. Indications FDA-Approved Indications Mifepristone, also known as RU-486, has 2 main FDA-approved indications. These are pregnancy termination combined with misoprostol through 10 weeks gestation and the management and treatment of hyperglycemia in patients exhibiting signs of Cushing syndrome.[1][2][3] Off-Label Uses In addition to the above indications, mifepristone has shown efficacy with off-label uses for postcoital emergency contraception, cervical maturation, and adjunct therapy for uterine leiomyomas.[2][4][5][6] Mechanism of Action Mifepristone works by antagonism of glucocorticoid and progesterone receptors. At low doses, mifepristone works by being a selective antagonist of progesterone. The drug does so by binding to the intracellular progesterone receptor. At high doses, mifepristone blocks cortisol at the glucocorticoid receptor. This action causes an effect on the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, leading to an increase in circulating cortisol, thus controlling hyperglycemia in some patients. Mifepristone has a higher affinity for the glucocorticoid II receptor than the glucocorticoid I receptor. For use in pregnancy termination, mifepristone works by interrupting progesterone. Progesterone is the primary hormone in preparing the endometrium for implantation and sensitizing the body to the effects of prostaglandins by increasing their synthesis and decreasing their metabolism. It causes the release of endogenous prostaglandins and an increase in the sensitivity of the myometrium to the contractile effects of prostaglandins. The increase in prostaglandins results in menstrual bleeding, disruption of the endometrium, and then termination.[1][7] Pharmacokinetics Absorption: Mifepristone is rapidly absorbed, and peak plasma concentrations are attained 90 minutes after administration. Distribution: Mifepristone has high plasma protein binding (approximately 98%); it binds to albumin and alpha-1-acid glycoprotein. Mifepristone can cross the blood-brain barrier.[8] Metabolism: Mifepristone is metabolized by CYP3A4, CY2C8, CYP2C9, and CYP2B6; it forms pharmacologically active metabolites.[9][10] Elimination: The average elimination half-life of mifepristone is 18 hours (single dose). The primary route of elimination is through feces.[11][12] Administration Available Dosage Forms Mifepristone is generally available as an oral tablet in 200 mg and 300 mg preparations. Adult Dosing Clinicians should be enrolled in the REMS program. According to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) guidelines for medication abortion, mifepristone can be used in the first 70 days (10 weeks) of gestation; clinicians should confirm pregnancy and estimate gestational age. Any intrauterine device present must be removed before initiating mifepristone. The regimen for termination of pregnancy involves a single mifepristone dose of 200 mg orally and misoprostol 800 μg buccally. Initially, a 200 mg tablet of mifepristone is administered in a single oral dose. On days 2 or 3, misoprostol should be placed in the buccal pouch as 4 200 μg tablets (total 800 μg). Misoprostol should be taken within 24 to 48 hours after taking mifepristone. Misoprostol should be kept in cheek pouches for at least 30 minutes. fetched_contents.text: Safety and effectiveness of self-managed medication abortion provided using online telemedicine in the United States: A population based study Summary Background As access to clinical abortion care becomes increasingly restricted in the United States, the need for self-managed abortions (i.e. abortions taking place outside of the formal healthcare setting) may increase. We examine the safety, effectiveness, and acceptability of self-managed medication abortion provided using online telemedicine. Methods We retrospectively examined records of the outcomes of abortions provided by the sole online telemedicine service providing self-managed medication abortion in the U.S. We calculated the prevalence of successful medication abortion (the proportion who ended their pregnancy without surgical intervention); the prevalence of serious adverse events (the proportions who received intravenous antibiotics and blood transfusion); and assessed whether any deaths were reported to the service. We also examined the proportions who were satisfied and felt self-management was the right choice. Findings Between March 20th 2018 and March 20th 2019, abortion medications were mailed to 4,584 people and 3,186 (70%) provided follow-up information. Among these, 2,797 (88%) confirmed use of the medications and provided outcome information, while 389 (12%) confirmed non-use. Overall, 96.4% (95% CI 95.7% to 97.1%) of those who used the medications reported successfully ending their pregnancy without surgical intervention and 1.0% (CI 0.7%-1.5%) reported treatment for any serious adverse event. Among these, 0.6% (CI 0.4% to 1.0%) reported receiving a blood transfusion, and 0.5% (CI 0.3% to 0.9%) reported receiving intravenous antibiotics. No deaths were reported to the service by family, friends, the authorities, or the media. Among 2,268 who provided information about their experience, 98.4% were satisfied and 95.5% felt self-management was the right choice. Interpretation Self-managed medication abortion provided using online telemedicine can be highly effective with low rates of serious adverse events. In light of increasingly restricted access to in-clinic abortion in the U.S., it may offer a safe and effective option for those who cannot access clinical care. Funding The Society of Family Planning and The National Institutes of Health. Keywords: Abortion, Self-managed, Online telemedicine, United States ---------------------------------------- Research in context. Evidence before this study In many U.S. states, access to abortion in the clinic setting is becoming increasingly restricted. In the face of dwindling access, there is evidence that people in the United States are self-managing their abortions (i.e. sourcing and conducting them outside of the formal healthcare setting). While self-managed abortions have been happening in North America for centuries using botanicals, and later misoprostol, one important contemporary method of self-management is the use of online telemedicine to provide the abortion medications mifepristone and misoprostol. No studies, however, have examined the safety, effectiveness, and acceptability of self-managed medication abortion using this model in the United States. We conducted a systematic search of MEDLINE and PubMed using the MeSH terms ‘Abortion’, ‘Self-managed’, ‘United States’, ‘Safety’ and ‘Effectiveness’ with no language or date restrictions, and found no relevant reports as of September 2021. Using data from the sole online telemedicine organization that provides self-managed medication abortion to people in the United States, we provide here an analysis of the reported outcomes of self-managed abortions provided between March 20th 2018 and March 20th 2019. We report both the proportion that resulted in successful termination of pregnancy and the proportion that resulted in serious adverse events. We also describe the acceptability of these self-managed abortions based on user experience. Added value of this study This study presents the first evidence that self-managed medication abortion provided through online telemedicine in the United States is effective, acceptable to users, and has a very low rate of serious adverse outcomes. This evidence adds to a global body of data showing that self-managed medication abortion is safe and effective. In this study, 70% of those to whom medications were shipped provided follow-up information about their abortions, and among these 2,797 (88%) confirmed use of the medications and provided outcome information, while 389 (12%) confirmed non-use. Among those who used the medications, 96% were able to end their pregnancies without surgical intervention from a clinical provider, a rate comparable with the in-clinic setting. Treatment for serious adverse events was uncommon with 1% receiving a blood transfusion or intravenous antibiotics. No deaths were reported to the service by family, friends, the authorities, or the media. Among the 2,268 people who provided information about their experience, 98% expressed satisfaction with their abortion experience and 96% said it was the right choice. Implications of all the available evidence As restrictive abortion legislation continues to create substantial barriers to in-clinic abortion in many U.S. states, abortion self-managed outside of the formal healthcare setting is an important option for those who cannot or prefer not to access clinical care. This study provides key evidence for clinicians, policymakers, and the public that safe, effective, self-managed medication abortion is available in the United States. However, people who self-manage are still vulnerable to legal risks and in some states unjust prosecutions have occurred. Rather than being subject to criminalization, self-managed abortion should be a legitimate part of a spectrum of options for abortion care that must be made available in the United States. ## Medically induced abortion compared with other abortion options

Medically induced abortion is one of two main types of early abortion care, along with surgical abortion. The key difference is that medically induced abortion uses medication rather than a surgical procedure to end a pregnancy [N1-R1][N1-R2]. In medically induced abortion, the process typically involves two medications: **mifepristone** and **misoprostol** [N1-F1][N3-F4]. Mifepristone works by blocking progesterone, the hormone that supports pregnancy, while misoprostol triggers uterine contractions and cervical softening [N2-F2][N2-F3]. Together, they stop the pregnancy and cause the body to expel the tissue [N1-F1][N2-F2].

### How it differs from surgical abortion
Surgical abortion is a small operation that removes the pregnancy through the cervix, usually using gentle suction. It may be done under general anesthesia, sedation, or local anesthesia, and the procedure itself is typically quick, lasting about 10 minutes [N1-F1]. Surgical abortion is usually used when medically induced abortion is not an option, such as later in pregnancy, or when a provider decides that surgery is safer for a patient [N1-F1].

### How it differs from “medical abortion”
“Medical abortion” is a shorthand term for medically induced abortion, and in many sources it is used interchangeably with medication abortion [N1-R3][N1-F1]. The distinction in the evidence is subtle: “medical abortion” is sometimes used as a general category, while the more precise term “medically induced abortion” emphasizes the use of medication rather than surgery [N1-R1][N1-F1]. In practice, this means that “medical abortion” and “medically induced abortion” refer to the same process, with the latter being the more formal or precise description.

### When each option is typically used
Medically induced abortion is typically used for early pregnancy, up to about 70 days (10 weeks) of gestation [N2-F2][N4-R2][N4-R5]. It is often preferred when a patient wants a non-surgical option, especially for pregnancies within the gestational limit [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Surgical abortion is generally used for pregnancies beyond that limit, or when medically induced abortion is not appropriate for the patient’s health or circumstances [N1-F1].

### Relative advantages and disadvantages for patients
A major advantage of medically induced abortion is that it can often be done outside a clinic setting, either at home or with some at-home medication management [N1-F1]. It is also less invasive and may be preferred by patients who want to avoid surgery [N1-F1][N2-F2]. A major disadvantage is that it can be more physically uncomfortable, with stronger cramping, heavier bleeding, and longer recovery than some surgical options [N1-F1][N2-F3]. It is also usually limited to early pregnancy [N2-F2][N4-R2].

Overall, medically induced abortion is usually a good option for early pregnancy when a patient prefers a non-surgical approach and is within the gestational limit [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Surgical abortion is typically used when medically induced abortion is not suitable, especially later in pregnancy, or when a provider prefers a more immediate procedure [N1-F1].

## Risks, side effects, and what patients should expect

### Common symptoms and side effects during and after the process
Patients undergoing medically induced abortion commonly experience cramping, heavy bleeding, and passing blood clots [N1-F1][N2-F3]. Bleeding and cramping may begin within an hour to four hours after taking misoprostol, and heavier cramping and bleeding can continue afterward [N2-F3]. Other common side effects include headache, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fatigue, and tiredness [N1-F1][N5-R1]. These symptoms are usually uncomfortable but are generally expected and temporary [N1-F1][N5-R1].

Patients may also feel tired for one to two days after misoprostol use, and most people return to normal activities the day after the process [N5-R1][N5-R4]. The Cleveland Clinic notes that symptoms often settle and improve within 4–6 hours, although some people may take longer [N1-F1]. Planned Parenthood similarly says most people return to normal activity the day after the process [N5-R1].

### Warning signs that require immediate medical attention
There are some warning signs that patients should watch for and seek urgent care if they occur. These include:
- **Excessive bleeding**, such as soaking through a pad every hour or needing to change pads frequently [N1-F1]
- **Severe pain** that is not relieved by painkillers [N1-F1]
- **Signs of infection**, such as fever, chills, or foul-smelling discharge [N2-F2]
- **Signs of retained products**, such as ongoing heavy bleeding or continued cramping after the expected time [N3-R3]
- **Shock-like symptoms**, such as dizziness, fainting, or a rapid heartbeat [N2-F2]

The evidence also notes that serious adverse events can occur, though they are uncommon: 1% of users in a large online telemedicine study required treatment for serious adverse events, including blood transfusions or intravenous antibiotics, and no deaths were reported [N3-F4]. Patients should call a provider or go to an emergency room if they experience any of these signs [N1-F1][N2-F2].

### What follow-up care is usually needed
Follow-up care is an important part of medically induced abortion. Patients are usually asked to return for a pregnancy test 14 or 21 days after the procedure to confirm successful termination [N1-F1]. Follow-up care also includes monitoring for complications and ensuring that the abortion was complete [N1-F1][N3-F4].

In addition, patients should keep their provider informed if symptoms do not improve or get worse, especially if bleeding is heavy or pain is severe [N2-F2]. Some sources emphasize that patients should follow their provider’s instructions carefully and report any unusual symptoms promptly [N1-F1][N3-F4]. Planned Parenthood also notes that patients should take painkillers as needed and can use ibuprofen or paracetamol up to the recommended safe dose [N1-F1].

Overall, medically induced abortion is usually a safe procedure, but patients should be aware of common side effects, recognize warning signs, and follow up as instructed to ensure the best outcome [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F4].

## Legal, ethical, and access-related context

### Legal restrictions or requirements by country or region
The evidence provided here is not country-specific in detail, but it does show that laws and policies around abortion vary significantly and can restrict access. The evidence notes that policies restricting access to abortion can delay or deny essential evidence-based medical care and that abortion bans and other restrictions violate long-established medical ethics [N6-R2][N6-R3]. It also highlights that in the U.S., restrictive abortion legislation has created substantial barriers to in-clinic abortion in many states [N6-R1]. In some states, abortion access is further constrained by laws that restrict where and how providers can offer care [N6-R3].

The evidence also points to broader reproductive governance and the “chilling effect” of restrictive laws on access, which can reduce access to induced abortion through clinical and administrative barriers [N6-R5]. While the specific gestational age limits in the provided evidence are not tied to a single country, the broader implication is that legal restrictions can vary by region and can make abortion care more difficult to obtain [N6-R1][N6-R5].

### Ethical considerations and patient autonomy
Ethically, medically induced abortion is supported as a legitimate medical procedure that respects patient autonomy and choice. The evidence explicitly states that abortion bans and other restrictions violate long-established medical ethical standards [N6-R2]. It also notes that defensive medicine and hesitant medicine arise when providers alter care to avoid criminal charges in a dynamic legal environment, which can undermine patient care [N6-R3]. This means that legal restrictions can interfere with ethical care by creating fear, hesitation, and inconsistent standards of practice [N6-R2][N6-R3].

In practice, medically induced abortion is part of a spectrum of options, and patient autonomy is central to decision-making. The evidence emphasizes that self-managed medication abortion can be safe and effective when done under appropriate guidance, and that patients should be able to access care without criminalization [N6-R5]. Ethically, providers should support patients in making informed choices and should not be constrained by laws that suppress evidence-based care [N6-R2].

### Barriers to access and how they affect care
The evidence shows that barriers to access can be substantial and can affect care in several ways. Restrictive abortion policies can delay or deny care, which can worsen health outcomes and increase complications [N6-R1]. In the U.S., increasingly restrictive access has led to greater reliance on self-managed abortion, including online telemedicine, as in-clinic care becomes harder to access [N6-R1][N6-R5]. While self-managed medication abortion can be effective and low-risk in some settings, it also exposes patients to legal risks and can create vulnerability to unjust prosecutions [N6-R5].

Barriers can also affect the quality of care. The evidence notes that abortion bans create hesitant medicine, where providers alter care to avoid legal consequences [N6-R3]. This can reduce trust, reduce care quality, and reduce access to timely and appropriate services [N6-R1][N6-R3]. Overall, legal and access barriers can make abortion care less available, less timely, and more stressful for patients, while also placing providers in difficult ethical and legal situations [N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R5].

## Concise patient-oriented explanation of medically induced abortion

Medically induced abortion is a non-surgical way to end an early pregnancy using medication rather than surgery [N1-R1][N1-R2]. It is also often called “medical abortion,” though the more precise term emphasizes the use of medicine [N1-R3][N1-F1]. The process usually involves two medications: **mifepristone** and **misoprostol** [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Mifepristone blocks the hormone progesterone, which supports pregnancy, while misoprostol causes the uterus to contract and the cervix to soften, helping the body expel the pregnancy [N2-F2][N2-F3].

### How it works step by step

# What is “aborto medico,” and what should you know?

## What “aborto medico” means
“Aborto medico” is a term used in Spanish to refer to **medically induced abortion**, which is a non-surgical way to end an early pregnancy using medication rather than surgery [N1-R1][N1-R2]. In many sources, it is also called **medical abortion** or **medication abortion** [N1-R3][N1-F1]. The process typically involves two medications: **mifepristone** and **misoprostol** [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Together, they stop the pregnancy and help the body expel the tissue [N1-F1][N2-F3].

### How it works
1. **First medication**: Mifepristone is taken by mouth. It blocks the hormone progesterone, which supports pregnancy [N2-F2][N2-F3].
2. **Second medication**: Misoprostol is taken later, usually 36 to 48 hours after mifepristone. It causes cramping and bleeding, and helps the pregnancy pass from the body [N1-F1][N2-F3].
3. **What happens afterward**: The pregnancy tissue usually passes out of the body with bleeding and cramping. Most people can return to normal activity the day after the process [N1-F1][N5-R1].

## How it differs from other abortion options
There are two main types of abortion care: **medically induced abortion** and **surgical abortion** [N1-R1][N1-R2].  
- **Medically induced abortion** uses medication to end the pregnancy [N1-R1].  
- **Surgical abortion** is a small operation that removes the pregnancy through the cervix, usually using gentle suction [N1-F1].  

In the evidence provided, **“medical abortion”** is used as a shorthand for medically induced abortion [N1-R3][N1-F1]. So, “aborto medico” is essentially the same as medically induced abortion, though the term is more precise when discussing the use of medication rather than surgery [N1-R1][N1-F1].

### When each option is typically used
- **Medically induced abortion** is usually used for early pregnancy, up to about 70 days (10 weeks) of gestation [N2-F2][N4-R2][N4-R5].  
- **Surgical abortion** is generally used when medically induced abortion is not appropriate, such as later in pregnancy, or when a provider decides surgery is safer for the patient [N1-F1].  

### Relative advantages and disadvantages
A major advantage of medically induced abortion is that it can often be done outside a clinic setting, either at home or with some at-home medication management [N1-F1]. It is also less invasive and may be preferred by patients who want to avoid surgery [N1-F1][N2-F2].  
A major disadvantage is that it can be more physically uncomfortable, with stronger cramping, heavier bleeding, and longer recovery than some surgical options [N1-F1][N2-F3]. It is also usually limited to early pregnancy [N2-F2][N4-R2].  

## What you should expect
### Common symptoms and side effects
Patients undergoing medically induced abortion commonly experience:
- **Cramping**
- **Heavy bleeding**
- **Passing blood clots**
- **Headache**
- **Nausea**
- **Vomiting**
- **Diarrhea**
- **Fatigue**
- **Tiredness**

These symptoms are usually uncomfortable but are generally expected and temporary [N1-F1][N5-R1][N2-F3]. Most people feel tired for one to two days after taking misoprostol, and many return to normal activity the day after the process [N5-R1][N5-R4]. The Cleveland Clinic notes that symptoms often settle and improve within 4–6 hours, though some people may take longer [N1-F1].

### Warning signs that require immediate medical attention
You should contact a provider or go to an emergency room if you experience:
- **Excessive bleeding**, such as soaking through a pad every hour or needing to change pads frequently [N1-F1]
- **Severe pain** that is not relieved by painkillers [N1-F1]
- **Signs of infection**, such as fever, chills, or foul-smelling discharge [N2-F2]
- **Signs of retained products**, such as ongoing heavy bleeding or continued cramping after the expected time [N3-R3]
- **Shock-like symptoms**, such as dizziness, fainting, or a rapid heartbeat [N2-F2]

A large study found that serious adverse events were uncommon: 1% of users required treatment for serious adverse events, including blood transfusions or intravenous antibiotics, and no deaths were reported [N3-F4]. That means medically induced abortion is usually very safe, but it is still important to recognize warning signs and act quickly if they occur [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F4].

### What follow-up care is usually needed
Follow-up care is an important part of medically induced abortion. Patients are usually asked to return for a pregnancy test 14 or 21 days after the procedure to confirm successful termination [N1-F1]. Follow-up care also includes monitoring for complications and ensuring that the abortion was complete [N1-F1][N3-F4].  
You should also keep your provider informed if symptoms do not improve or get worse, especially if bleeding is heavy or pain is severe [N2-F2]. Planned Parenthood also says patients should take painkillers as needed and can use ibuprofen or paracetamol up to the recommended safe dose [N1-F1].

## Who can provide medically induced abortion and when it is available
### Gestational age limits
Medically induced abortion is typically offered up to about 70 days (10 weeks) of gestation [N2-F2][N4-R2][N4-R5]. Some evidence suggests that gestational age limits can be extended beyond 70 days, but the standard guidance here is that the medication regimen is approved through 10 weeks [N4-R2][N4-R5]. Outside that window, the evidence provided does not give a full eligibility framework, so the safest patient-oriented summary is the approved limit [N2-F2][N4-R2].

### Conditions that make someone ineligible
Not all patients are eligible for medically induced abortion. ACOG notes that there are medical conditions for which medication abortion is not appropriate [N4-R1]. The evidence also indicates that patients may need to be assessed for eligibility before starting the process, and that some patients may be asked to take the medications in a clinic or hospital if they have medical conditions or if home use is not safe [N1-F1]. The specific ineligibility criteria are not fully detailed in the provided material, but the key point is that eligibility depends on pregnancy timing and medical suitability [N4-R1][N1-F1].

### Provider qualifications and settings
Providers who offer medically induced abortion should be trained or able to refer to a clinician who can perform uterine evacuation if needed [N7-R2]. ACOG’s guidance also emphasizes that clinicians should be enrolled in the REMS program and should confirm pregnancy and estimate gestational age [N2-F2]. In addition, care can be provided in a clinic setting, and some programs may offer home-based or self-managed options, but with careful provider supervision and follow-up [N1-F1][N3-F4].

## Legal, ethical, and access-related context
### Legal restrictions or requirements
The evidence shows that abortion laws and policies vary and can restrict access. Policies restricting access can delay or deny essential evidence-based medical care and can violate long-established medical ethics [N6-R2][N6-R3]. In the U.S., restrictive abortion legislation has created substantial barriers to in-clinic abortion in many states [N6-R1]. In some states, abortion access is further constrained by laws that restrict where and how providers can offer care [N6-R3].  
The evidence also points to broader reproductive governance and the “chilling effect” of restrictive laws on access, which can reduce access to induced abortion through clinical and administrative barriers [N6-R5]. While the specific gestational age limits in the provided evidence are not tied to a single country, the broader implication is that legal restrictions can vary by region and can make abortion care more difficult to obtain [N6-R1][N6-R5].

### Ethical considerations
Ethically, medically induced abortion is supported as a legitimate medical procedure that respects patient autonomy and choice. The evidence explicitly states that abortion bans and other restrictions violate long-established medical ethical standards [N6-R2]. It also notes that defensive medicine and hesitant medicine arise when providers alter care to avoid criminal charges in a dynamic legal environment, which can undermine patient care [N6-R3]. This means that legal restrictions can interfere with ethical care by creating fear, hesitation, and inconsistent standards of practice [N6-R2][N6-R3].

### Barriers to access
The evidence shows that barriers to access can be substantial and can affect care in several ways. Restrictive abortion policies can delay or deny care, which can worsen health outcomes and increase complications [N6-R1]. In the U.S., increasingly restrictive access has led to greater reliance on self-managed abortion, including online telemedicine, as in-clinic care becomes harder to access [N6-R1][N6-R5]. While self-managed medication abortion can be safe and effective in some settings, it also exposes patients to legal risks and can create vulnerability to unjust prosecutions [N6-R5].  
Barriers can also affect the quality of care. The evidence notes that abortion bans create hesitant medicine, where providers alter care to avoid legal consequences [N6-R3]. This can reduce trust, reduce care quality, and reduce access to timely and appropriate services [N6-R1][N6-R3]. Overall, legal and access barriers can make abortion care less available, less timely, and more stressful for patients, while also placing providers in difficult ethical and legal situations [N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R5].

## Bottom line
If you have “aborto medico” on your mind, it is most likely medically induced abortion: a non-surgical option for ending an early pregnancy using medication [N1-R1][N1-F1]. It is usually done with mifepristone and misoprostol, and it is typically available up to about 10 weeks of pregnancy [N2-F2][N4-R2][N4-R5]. It is generally safe and effective, but it can be uncomfortable and is not suitable for everyone [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-R1]. If you are considering this option, speak with a provider who can assess your pregnancy, check your medical suitability, and explain the process and follow-up care [N1-F1][N2-F2][N7-R2]. And if you are in a place where access is limited, legal restrictions or access barriers may affect how you receive care [N6-R1][N6-R5].

## Concise patient-oriented explanation of medically induced abortion

Medically induced abortion is a non-surgical way to end an early pregnancy using medication rather than surgery [N1-R1][N1-R2]. It is also often called “medical abortion,” though the more precise term emphasizes the use of medicine [N1-R3][N1-F1]. The process usually involves two medications: **mifepristone** and **misoprostol** [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Mifepristone blocks the hormone progesterone, which supports pregnancy, while misoprostol causes the uterus to contract and the cervix to soften, helping the body expel the pregnancy [N2-F2][N2-F3].

### How it works step by step
1. **First medication**: Mifepristone is taken by mouth. It stops the pregnancy from continuing by blocking progesterone [N2-F2][N2-F3].
2. **Second medication**: Misoprostol is taken later, usually 36 to 48 hours after mifepristone. It causes cramping and bleeding, and helps the pregnancy pass from the body [N1-F1][N2-F3].
3. **What happens afterward**: The pregnancy tissue usually passes out of the body with bleeding and cramping. Most people can return to normal activity the day after the process [N1-F1][N5-R1].

### When it is available
Medically induced abortion is typically available for pregnancies up to about 70 days (10 weeks) of gestation [N2-F2][N4-R2][N4-R5]. In some cases, it may also be used later, but the evidence here focuses on the standard early-gestation window [N4-R5]. It is usually available in clinics, and some programs may offer at-home or self-managed options, but providers usually give instructions carefully before starting the process [N1-F1].

### What the provider needs to do
The provider should:
- Confirm the pregnancy and estimate gestational age [N2-F2]
- Check for medical conditions that might make medically induced abortion less safe or unsuitable [N4-R1]
- Provide instructions on how to take the medications and when to take them [N1-F1]
- Arrange follow-up care to confirm the abortion was successful and to monitor for complications [N1-F1][N3-F4]
- Be trained to handle complications or refer to emergency care if needed [N7-R2]

In short, medically induced abortion is a non-surgical, medication-based option for early pregnancy, using mifepristone and misoprostol, usually available up to 10 weeks of gestation, with careful provider support and follow-up [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-R2][N7-R2].

A major disadvantage is that it can be more physically uncomfortable, with stronger cramping, heavier bleeding, and longer recovery than some surgical options [N1-F1][N2-F3]. It is also usually limited to early pregnancy [N2-F2][N4-R2].  

## What you should expect
### Common symptoms and side effects
Patients undergoing medically induced abortion commonly experience:
- **Cramping**
- **Heavy bleeding**
- **Passing blood clots**
- **Headache**
- **Nausea**
- **Vomiting**
- **Diarrhea**
- **Fatigue**
- **Tiredness**

These symptoms are usually uncomfortable but are generally expected and temporary [N1-F1][N5-R1][N2-F3]. Most people feel tired for one to two days after taking misoprostol, and many return to normal activity the day after the process [N5-R1][N5-R4]. The Cleveland Clinic notes that symptoms often settle and improve within 4–6 hours, though some people may take longer [N1-F1].

### Warning signs that require immediate medical attention
You should contact a provider or go to an emergency room if you experience:
- **Excessive bleeding**, such as soaking through a pad every hour or needing to change pads frequently [N1-F1]
- **Severe pain** that is not relieved by painkillers [N1-F1]
- **Signs of infection**, such as fever, chills, or foul-smelling discharge [N2-F2]
- **Signs of retained products**, such as ongoing heavy bleeding or continued cramping after the expected time [N3-R3]
- **Shock-like symptoms**, such as dizziness, fainting, or a rapid heartbeat [N2-F2]

A large study found that serious adverse events were uncommon: 1% of users required treatment for serious adverse events, including blood transfusions or intravenous antibiotics, and no deaths were reported [N3-F4]. That means medically induced abortion is usually very safe, but it is still important to recognize warning signs and act quickly if they occur [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F4].

### What follow-up care is usually needed
Follow-up care is an important part of medically induced abortion. Patients are usually asked to return for a pregnancy test 14 or 21 days after the procedure to confirm successful termination [N1-F1]. Follow-up care also includes monitoring for complications and ensuring that the abortion was complete [N1-F1][N3-F4].  
You should also keep your provider informed if symptoms do not improve or get worse, especially if bleeding is heavy or pain is severe [N2-F2]. Planned Parenthood also says patients should take painkillers as needed and can use ibuprofen or paracetamol up to the recommended safe dose [N1-F1].

## Who can provide medically induced abortion and when it is available
### Gestational age limits
Medically induced abortion is typically offered up to about 70 days (10 weeks) of gestation [N2-F2][N4-R2][N4-R5]. Some evidence suggests that gestational age limits can be extended beyond 70 days, but the standard guidance here is that the medication regimen is approved through 10 weeks [N4-R2][N4-R5]. Outside that window, the evidence provided does not give a full eligibility framework, so the safest patient-oriented summary is the approved limit [N2-F2][N4-R2].

### Conditions that make someone ineligible
Not all patients are eligible for medically induced abortion. ACOG notes that there are medical conditions for which medication abortion is not appropriate [N4-R1]. The evidence also indicates that patients may need to be assessed for eligibility before starting the process, and that some patients may be asked to take the medications in a clinic or hospital if they have medical conditions or if home use is not safe [N1-F1]. The specific ineligibility criteria are not fully detailed in the provided material, but the key point is that eligibility depends on pregnancy timing and medical suitability [N4-R1][N1-F1].

### Provider qualifications and settings
Providers who offer medically induced abortion should be trained or able to refer to a clinician who can perform uterine evacuation if needed [N7-R2]. ACOG’s guidance also emphasizes that clinicians should be enrolled in the REMS program and should confirm pregnancy and estimate gestational age [N2-F2]. In addition, care can be provided in a clinic setting, and some programs may offer home-based or self-managed options, but with careful provider supervision and follow-up [N1-F1][N3-F4].

## Legal, ethical, and access-related context
### Legal restrictions or requirements
The evidence shows that abortion laws and policies vary and can restrict access. Policies restricting access can delay or deny essential evidence-based medical care and can violate long-established medical ethics [N6-R2][N6-R3]. In the U.S., restrictive abortion legislation has created substantial barriers to in-clinic abortion in many states [N6-R1]. In some states, abortion access is further constrained by laws that restrict where and how providers can offer care [N6-R3].  
The evidence also points to broader reproductive governance and the “chilling effect” of restrictive laws on access, which can reduce access to induced abortion through clinical and administrative barriers [N6-R5]. While the specific gestational age limits in the provided evidence are not tied to a single country, the broader implication is that legal restrictions can vary by region and can make abortion care more difficult to obtain [N6-R1][N6-R5].

### Ethical considerations
Ethically, medically induced abortion is supported as a legitimate medical procedure that respects patient autonomy and choice. The evidence explicitly states that abortion bans and other restrictions violate long-established medical ethical standards [N6-R2]. It also notes that defensive medicine and hesitant medicine arise when providers alter care to avoid criminal charges in a dynamic legal environment, which can undermine patient care [N6-R3]. This means that legal restrictions can interfere with ethical care by creating fear, hesitation, and inconsistent standards of practice [N6-R2][N6-R3].

### Barriers to access
The evidence shows that barriers to access can be substantial and can affect care in several ways. Restrictive abortion policies can delay or deny care, which can worsen health outcomes and increase complications [N6-R1]. In the U.S., increasingly restrictive access has led to greater reliance on self-managed abortion, including online telemedicine, as in-clinic care becomes harder to access [N6-R1][N6-R5]. While self-managed medication abortion can be safe and effective in some settings, it also exposes patients to legal risks and can create vulnerability to unjust prosecutions [N6-R5].  
Barriers can also affect the quality of care. The evidence notes that abortion bans create hesitant medicine, where providers alter care to avoid legal consequences [N6-R3]. This can reduce trust, reduce care quality, and reduce access to timely and appropriate services [N6-R1][N6-R3]. Overall, legal and access barriers can make abortion care less available, less timely, and more stressful for patients, while also placing providers in difficult ethical and legal situations [N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R5].

## Bottom line
If you have “aborto medico” on your mind, it is most likely medically induced abortion: a non-surgical option for ending an early pregnancy using medication [N1-R1][N1-F1]. It is usually done with mifepristone and misoprostol, and it is typically available up to about 10 weeks of pregnancy [N2-F2][N4-R2][N4-R5]. It is generally safe and effective, but it can be uncomfortable and is not suitable for everyone [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-R1]. If you are considering this option, speak with a provider who can assess your pregnancy, check your medical suitability, and explain the process and follow-up care [N1-F1][N2-F2][N7-R2]. And if you are in a place where access is limited, legal restrictions or access barriers may affect how you receive care [N6-R1][N6-R5].
